about: The words of the chain coast_watch_810 (Data/encounters/chain_coast_watch_810_793.json; Design/content/chains/coast_watch_810.md): the emperor's coast watch and the Danish king's two hundred ships, 808 to 812. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the three news items the endings post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Count Folcbert (cast.folcbert) and his clerk; Gerwin, who keeps the watch at Walichrum; Sibrand, law-speaker of the mound at Emuthon, the widow Tetta and her grandson Sibo; Ketil, a ship's chief of the Danish fleet; Baldric, the wright at Ganda (all invented, attested name parts); the old Dane of the crew is cast.crew.ravn. Nothing here is quoted from any book: the annals and Einhard are told in our own words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The watch roll

On the dam at Dorestat the count's clerk stands on a cask and reads an order of the emperor to anyone who will stop. Boats and men are wanted for a watch on the river mouths. The count walks along the row of keels behind him, and stops at yours.

The lord emperor orders that ships be made ready along the shore of the sea, and that a watch be kept at every harbour and river mouth where a ship can come in. It is not the first time he has ordered it.

The law for you Frisians is simple. Men with horses come themselves. Of the rest, six find the seventh man his bread and his spear, and the seventh goes. I need the seventh. I also need what he will stand in.
The Danish king burned a market of the Wends last summer and carried its merchants home in his ships like hens in a basket. He has more ships than he has uses for.
Count Egbert is building a fort beyond the Elbe this spring. The Danish king will take it as it is meant.
Well, shipman. Your boat is small, but she floats, which is more than I can say for some of what I have been sent.
Put your boat on the watch roll
Pay your part of a seventh man and keep your summer
Say the boat is too small to stop anything, and ask what the watch is for

The clerk writes the boat down under the count's eye, and the toll man is told to go easy on a keel that serves. Your post is the mouth of the Scheldt, at Walichrum, where a man named Gerwin keeps the fire. You are to show yourself there before the summer is out.

Twenty pennies go into the count's chest toward a spear and a sack of bread for a man you will never meet. The clerk gives you a notched stick to prove it. The post is at Walichrum, he says, if you should ever wish to see what you bought.

The count has already walked on. The clerk answers instead, quietly. The watch is a fire on a dune and some boats beside it: at Walichrum, at the mouth of the Maas, at the Vlie. It is for seeing a fleet. What happens after a fleet is seen, the order does not say.
Four boats on the sand

On the highest dune at Walichrum there is a pile of driftwood under a cowhide, kept dry to burn. Below it four boats lie on the sand. Two of them are flat river barges with their noses pointed bravely at the sea.
Four boats. Two were built to carry dung down the Scheldt, and they have not forgotten it. In anything of a wind they go sideways.
The emperor ordered a fleet in the year he rode to Rome. I have had orders every year since. If orders were oak I could plank the sea from here to Britain.
I have a field on the far side of the island. Six neighbours feed me so that they need not come. I am the seventh part of a soldier, and it is hay time.
You are on the count's roll. Good. That makes five boats, and the first that can turn.

If I light that fire, the next fire is lit at the abbey's landing, and by the second night the count knows. By then whoever came is home again and counting. Somebody up the river should be told that. They do not read what I send.
Stand a week on the watch with your boat
Carry his letter up the river: the watch can see a fleet, not stop one
Sell them bread and ale and say nothing about the barges

Seven days lying off the bar in the grey, and seven nights taking turns by an unlit fire. You see fishermen, a porpoise, and a monk in a boat who is lost. Gerwin pays you the count's ration money, twenty-four pennies, and says it is the first week all summer he has slept.

He has it written by the priest on the back of an old tally: four boats, two unfit, thirty men of whom nine have held a spear, and a fire. He gives you ten pennies for the carrying. At Dorestat the clerk takes it, reads it, and puts it with others.
Men on a dune are a good market. They pay thirty pennies for what would fetch twenty anywhere with a roof, and Gerwin thanks you for coming, since nobody else does.
Rope for two hundred keels

The landing is full of ships that are not trading. Men are stepping masts, turning shields over to look at the straps, and carrying bread aboard by the sack. A man with a gilded pin walks down the shingle to see what a Frisian keel is doing among them.
A Frisian keel. The king likes merchants; he sends his messages by them. So I ask as a friend. Whose man are you this summer?
Every rope walk on this coast is sold out to the last fathom. Rope, tar, bread that keeps. The king is buying for two hundred keels, and he pays in silver he took from the Wends.

I know three of those ships. I know their steersmen too. Now look at the sacks going aboard. I gave up counting them. Nobody carries that much bread to cross a bay. That is bread for going somewhere and coming back.

The king says Frisia is his own land and Saxony too, and that the emperor may keep them warm for him. He says he will come to Aachen himself one day and see whether the hall is as big as they tell it.
Buy the ale and let your Dane ask his questions
Sell the king's buyers bread and rope at their price
Say you are nobody's man, and trade as on any other day

Six pennies of ale and one evening. Your Dane listens, and comes back with all of it. Two hundred ships. Not for the Wends this time: west, along the islands, when the barley is in ear and the sea has settled. The king will stay at home. They want silver and cattle, and to be back for harvest.

They take everything in the hold that can be eaten or tied, weigh out a hundred and forty pennies' worth of hack-silver without arguing, and tell you why they are in a hurry: the fleet goes west along the Frisian islands when the barley is in ear. The king's man says he will know your boat again. He means it kindly.
He looks at you for the time it takes to count a crew, and goes back up the shingle. Nobody's man is told nothing. You trade as on any other day, on a day that is not like any other.
A rumour is not a cargo
The mound is at its spring work. Ewes and lambs are out on the salt grass and there is washed wool on every fence. Nobody here has heard anything from the north, and nobody is looking that way.
The count's man was here at Candlemas. He counted our boats, wrote down the number, and went away again. We have not been told what the number was for.
My man went to the host in the Saxon years, and the host kept him. I have forty ewes and no wish for news. News has never once brought me a ewe.
You are standing like a man with a hot stone in his hand, looking for somewhere to put it down.
The sun went dark three weeks after Pentecost, in the forenoon. The old women have been telling us what it meant ever since. They do not agree, so I suppose we shall find out.
Tell them what you heard in the Danes' harbour: two hundred keels, this summer
Tell them to send to the count for men, as the law says
Trade and keep your news to yourself

The law-speaker hears you out and asks one question: who told you. Then he sends boys over the flats to the next mounds at low water. By evening the cattle are being driven inland to the high sand, and the women are taking off their brooches. The best of the silver goes down the well in a pot. It will not stop a fleet. It will leave a fleet less to carry.
A rider goes south with the message, since that is the law. He comes back in nine days. The count is with the host and the count's clerk has written the message down.
You sell what you came to sell, twenty pennies to the good, and they wish you a fair wind. From the water the mound looks as it has looked for three hundred years: a green hump, smoke, and sheep.
Sails to the north

To the north the edge of the sea has gone rough, like cloth with the nap raised. It is sails: more than any trading season ever put on the water, coming down along the islands under oar and sail together.
Sails. I stopped counting at sixty, and I had not come to the end of them.
The king's. Every one of them. Be easy. They want cattle and silver, and they want to be home for harvest. One small keel is not worth an hour of anybody's rowing.
Some of them are eating your bread at this moment. I hope it was good. I do, truly.
Unless she runs. That is the one thing, mind. A boat that runs has something aboard, and young men like a race.
Drop the sail and the mast and lie on the flats until dark
Put her before the wind and run for the river
Stand on, and hail the nearest ship in her own tongue

With the mast down she is a log on a sandbank. The fleet goes by for most of the day, near enough to hear the oars. A gull sits on the stem. When the tide lifts you again it is dark, and the sea is empty and smells of tar.
She runs. Two of them turn after you, and give it up when the water under you goes pale and thin. A boat that draws a hand's breadth less has won, and your crew will be telling it for a year.
She runs, and a long ship with forty oars runs better. They come alongside laughing, take forty pennies' worth of silver out of your chest, weigh it carefully, and tell you that you row like Franks.

The nearest steersman shouts back that they are the king's ships and that the king is at home. Where are they bound? He points with his chin at the islands. Then he asks the price of cloth at Dorestat, hears it, shakes his head, and rows on.
The nearest ship understands you very well. A man who speaks the tongue can also be told plainly what he owes. Thirty pennies' worth, by their weights, and you are let go with good wishes.
A hundred pounds

Three fights have been lost. The Danes have laid a tribute on the whole coast, a hundred pounds of silver by weight, and each mound has been told its part. Emuthon's part is four pounds. That is nine hundred and sixty of the emperor's pennies, from people who keep sheep.
They beat us on Bant. They beat us at the creek. They beat us a third time, when we should have known better. Nobody came. We lit the fire, and it burned very well.
Four pounds. Our silver is on our women's shoulders and in two old graves. I have been speaker here thirty winters and I have never before had to ask whose grandmother was buried with what.
They have my son and eleven more sitting roped on the strand. It is to help us count faster.
It is paid. We paid with silver borrowed up the river against next summer's wool. Then the sickness came and the oxen died, every one. We owe for the tribute and we plough with cows.
We had your word and nine days. The cattle were on the high sand and the pot was in the well. They found less than they came for. They wanted their weight all the same.
The emperor's law has a name for the man who buys a hungry neighbour's goods for less than they are worth. It calls that foul gain. I have not found the law that says what the neighbour is to eat.
Put sixty pennies on the scale as your share, as if you lived here
Buy their cloth for ready silver, at a third of its worth
Keep your purse shut, and carry the women, the children and the ewes up the river

Sixty pennies, counted out on the law-speaker's cloak in front of the mound. Nobody thanks you. Sibrand cuts a notch in the tally of households, between the smith and the widow, and that is where your name now stands.

Six bolts of good Frisian cloth for ninety pennies, the work of two winters. The women carry it down to the boat themselves and stack it properly. It was their own offer, and it is lawful. Sibrand has it written down that it was lawful, with the day and your name.

Two days, three trips up the river to the high ground, with the boat full to the wash-strake of children, old women and ewes. One ewe is sick on your steersman. Tetta counts her flock off at the far end, twice, and says it is all there.
His weights

On the strand below the mound a Dane sits on a sea chest with a small folding balance. The mound's silver goes into one pan and his lead weights into the other. Behind him, by the boats, twelve men sit roped together and look at their feet.
Arm rings, brooches, a cup with a saint on it. Your pennies too. I do not mind whose face they carry. In the pan a king weighs the same as a nail.
My weights are honest. They are only heavier than yours. That is a difference between our countries, and I did not make it.
By his weights our four pounds is nearer five. I said so. He agreed with me, and went on weighing.
I know your boat. Your bread was good, and the rope has held. Sit down.
The king stayed at home this time. He says that next time he comes himself, with all of us, and goes on up the river to the emperor's hall. I only tell you what he says.
Buy the twelve roped men free at his price
Set your own Dorestat pound in the other pan, before everyone
Stand by, watch the weighing, and remember what he says of his king

Eighty pennies' weight for twelve men, which is cheap, and he says so: they are fishermen and would fetch little, and feeding them home costs bread. The rope is cut in one place and they walk up the mound in a line, still tied to each other, because nobody thinks to undo the rest.

You set the bronze pound from your own chest in his pan. It is stamped, and everybody on the strand can see the pan does not move as it should. He looks at it for a long breath. Then he laughs, takes one of his own weights out, and weighs the rest of the mound's silver against yours. It saves them most of a pound.

He picks your bronze pound out of his pan between two fingers, looks at the stamp, and drops it in his purse. A light weight is no use to an honest man, he says. Twenty pennies' worth of bronze and pride, and the weighing goes on as before.

You stand at the edge of it for half a day, as a merchant may, and you hear a good deal. He is called Ketil. The king is Godfred, who did not come and who talks of Aachen. The men like the silver. They are less sure about the king.
The host eats

The emperor has called out the host against the Danish king. Every boat on the river is wanted for bread, every cart is wanted for bacon, and anything an army eats costs half as much again as it did at Pentecost.

Bread that keeps. Bacon. Ale. Each man is to bring three months of food as far as the Saxon march, and the oxen that should haul it are lying dead along the road. So it comes by water, or it does not come.
Mine lay down between here and the ford and did not get up. They say a man from Benevento is going about the country with a bag of dust. I never saw him. I saw the oxen.

The host crossed at Lippeham, a day down the river. The emperor's elephant died there, the one the king of the Persians sent. All at once, between morning and noon. I saw it lying on the bank like a grey barn that had fallen over.
Word has come from the camp on the Weser. The fleet has gone home, and the Danish king is dead. One of his own following killed him. So the host has marched all this way to hear news.
Take the host's order for ship's bread
Hire the boat to the host for a fortnight's carrying
Stay clear of the host, and mark what bread is fetching

Eight sacks of hard bread, wanted here within forty days, at most of its price again on top. The provisioner cuts the tally himself and does not ask where you will find it. He has stopped asking anybody that.

A fortnight under another man's orders, up and down the river with sacks to the gunwale and a soldier sitting on them. A hundred and ten pennies at the end of it, counted out without a word. Your crew say they have carried quieter cattle.

A boat that goes near the host is pressed, and a pressed boat comes home at Martinmas. You keep to the far bank. But you mark the price: ship's bread is fetching nearly half as much again here, and will for a month yet.
Where was the watch?

The emperor's envoys are going down the coast with one question. At Dorestat one of them sits in the count's hall, in the count's chair, with a clerk beside him. The count stands. Shipmen are being called in from the dam, one at a time.

Two hundred ships came, took what they liked, and went home again. The lord emperor learned of it at Aachen from a man on a tired horse. He has had a watch ordered on this coast for ten years. I am to find out where it was.
The Frisians ran. Three times. Ask any man here.
A letter came up from Walichrum on the back of a tally. Four boats, two of them unfit. It was put with others. I have now read the others.
Shipman. You were on the water this summer, and you hold no land from anybody in this room. That makes you the nearest thing I have to a witness.
It is to be written in any case that oak is felled this winter, and ships are built on every river that runs into this sea.
Say what you saw: barges, farmers, and no lord within a day's ride of the boats
Say what the count says: the Frisians ran
Say you carry cloth, not opinions

You say it plainly. A fire on a dune. Barges. Men at hay time who are each one seventh of a soldier. Nobody with a sword and a horse nearer than a day. The clerk writes all the while. The count does not look at you, then or as you go out. He holds your house's debt, and you have just remembered it.

You say the Frisians ran. It is even true: on the third day they ran. The envoy looks at you a little longer than is comfortable and tells the clerk to write it. In the yard the count's man puts forty pennies in your hand, for your trouble in coming up from the dam.
The envoy says that is the answer he has had from every keel on the river, and that the emperor will be glad to know his merchants are so busy. The next man is called.
Three springs
The Danish king is dead by his own man's hand. His nephew Hemming has the high seat and wants peace. At Dorestat three men come to your fire in one week, and each of them has a use for your boat.

Ships are being built at Ganda on the Scheldt, and the emperor means to come and look at them himself before winter. The count wants men there who can tell one end of a keel from the other. He has found very few.
The count is not pleased with you. The envoy is. I should think about which of them lives nearer to your storehouse.
My father says the mound holds its meeting after the shearing. He says to tell you your name will be spoken at it. He did not say how.

Twelve men of each people are to swear the peace on the Eider. I speak Danish, so I go. But I am a Saxon, and a count's man, and neither side believes a word that comes out of me. They want somebody who has sold to both.
It should have been sworn already. The frost shut every road between us and them, so for now each side has sworn it at home, on its own weapons, and hopes the other did the same.
Go to Ganda in the autumn, for the emperor's ships
Go back to the mound at Emuthon after the shearing
Go north with the Saxon, to the swearing on the Eider

The clerk writes your name on a list that is shorter than he would like. Ganda, on the Scheldt, from Michaelmas. If you pass Quentovic on the way, he says, they are short of everything there too, and paying for it.
Sibrand's son nods as if he had been told you would say so. After the shearing, on the green by the creek. He goes back down the river the same day; there are cows to plough with.

The Saxon is plainly relieved. The Danish twelve will ride out from Sliesthorp, he says; be there when the roads open and ask for the spokesman of the king's brothers. Bring something to sell. Nobody trusts a merchant with an empty boat.
The old light

A day up the coast, at Bononia, the emperor's new ships are gathering under the old tower the Romans built. At Quentovic every pitch boiler and rope maker is working for the fleet, and the strand smells like the inside of a cask.
That tower has stood dark since the Romans went home. The emperor has had it mended, and a fire is to burn on top of it every night, for ships to steer by. Ours, he hopes.
The emperor has ordered that when the fleet sails, the lords go aboard themselves. I am a lord. I have been sick since the river mouth, and we have not yet left the river.
Pitch is what they are short of. Pitch, and men who have seen the sea before.
She is to be at Bononia before the emperor is. My steersman is a miller. A good miller. Would you take her up for me? I can pay, and I can keep out of the way.
Take the lord's ship up to Bononia for him
Take the fleet's order for pitch
Sail up at dusk and see the fire lit

Three days. She is long, new, stiff, and leaks at four strakes, and forty men pull forty different strokes. You bring her in under the tower on the evening flood with the lord sitting very still amidships. He pays a hundred and twenty pennies and asks you not to say who steered.
Six barrels of pitch, wanted here within forty-five days, at a good part of the price again on top. The harbour man says the emperor can order ships, but only a pine tree can make them float.

You stand off the cliffs at dusk. The tower is taller than any church, in bands of red and pale stone. A spark shows at the top, then a fire, then a light that lies on the water all the way out to you. Your crew say nothing for some time. Then the steersman says it will make the bar easier, at least.
The ships at Ganda

On the bank of the Scheldt at Ganda the new ships lie in a row, black with tar and still smelling of it. There are thirty of them. Shipwrights, monks, soldiers and the count's men stand about, waiting to be told who is to sail.
Thirty hulls in one year, out of oak that was standing at Easter. Half of them will open at the first hard frost. I have told the count's man. He asked me not to tell anyone taller.
He walked the whole row this morning. A very tall old man who favours one foot and will not be helped. He put his hand on every stem. At the last one he asked who would sail them.
Lords are to sail them, by his own order. Each lord goes aboard himself, with his own men. They are brave, and they have seen the sea from a hill.
I told him what a shipman said at Dorestat last autumn. He asked whether the shipman had anything better to offer than complaint. I said I would ask.
There is one hull over. We laid a keel too many, and I built her my own way while nobody was counting: deep, short, room for cargo. A trader's shape. He will not want her. She does not look fierce.
You have seen the light at Bononia, then. He likes old Roman things that can be made to work again. I wonder whether he counts himself among them.
Take your season's pay, and ask for the spare hull
Tell the envoy your idea: sworn Frisian shipmen on the watch, paid in toll freedom
Pilot the new ships down to the sea, take the count's silver and go home

Six hundred pennies for the season, and the hull nobody counted. Baldric has her written off as spoiled timber and helps you step the mast. The emperor's fleet goes down to the sea with lords aboard and is not much spoken of again. Yours goes down behind it, deep and short, and is the only one of the thirty-one that ever carries a cargo.

You say it to the envoy on the bank. Lords will come when they are called and go when the harvest calls louder. Shipmen live on this water. Swear the Frisian keels to the watch, forty days a summer each, in turns; pay them with freedom from the toll, which costs the emperor nothing he has in his hand. The envoy says it twice over to himself and goes up the row. He is gone until dusk. He comes back with twelve hundred pennies, a writing with a seal that frees your boat of the toll at Dorestat, and the first forty days, which are yours.

You take them down the Scheldt three at a time, with a lord in each stern and a boy in each bow calling the depth. None is lost. The count's man counts out nine hundred pennies and has you entered as the count's shipman: called first when the river needs a pilot, and paid first too. Then you go home, which is what the fleet does soon after.
The thing on the mound

The shearing is done, and the mound holds its meeting on the green by the creek. Peace has been sworn on the Eider. The oxen are dead and the wool is the best in years. Every household stands in its place, and there is a gap in the ring.
This meeting has three matters before it. A boundary stone that walks at night. A cow drowned in a neighbour's ditch. And you.

You put silver on the scale that you did not owe. I notched you into the tally between the smith and the widow. The smith has asked me whether that makes you his neighbour, and what you mean to do about his fence.
He carried my ewes up the river like guests at a wedding. One of them was sick on his steersman. I have brought the steersman a cheese.
My son is standing behind you. He has something to say to you and he will not manage it. He was one of the twelve.
You bought our cloth at a third when we could not say no. It was lawful. We wrote down that it was lawful. I read it out again this morning so that nobody should forget how lawful it was.
You brought the word before the ships came. No count did that. No count has done it yet.

We are done waiting for the emperor's boats. Next time there will be a fire ready on every mound from Bant to the Lauwers, and somebody awake beside it who is not somebody else's seventh man. The mounds are swearing it to each other this summer. What we lack is a keel to carry the word where a fire cannot be seen.
Is it true she can lie flat on the sand with her mast down, and nobody see her? I should like to see that. I mean, not see it.
Take the house plot they offer on the mound
Ask for a sworn man to keep your goods here instead
Swear into their watch: your boat carries the word between the fires, and the boy sails with you

The gap in the ring is yours: a house plot on the south side of the mound, twelve paces by thirty, above every tide anyone remembers. Fourteen bolts of this year's cloth are carried down to the boat to go with it. The coast pays its debts and mends its fences, and waits for the next sails, as it always has.

You would rather have a man than a house. They give you the smith's brother, who can count, and swear him on the meeting's own oath to keep your goods as his own. Six hundred and fifty pennies in silver and cut rings are laid on the cloak: the mound's thanks, weighed on your scale this time.

You swear with them, a hand on the meeting's staff: when a fire is lit, your keel carries the word past the next headland, whatever is in the hold. They give the plot, four hundred pennies in silver, and twenty bolts of cloth, which is most of a year's weaving. Tetta gives the boy. He is twelve, he can swim, and he is to come back knowing every bar from the Ems to the Rhine. That summer there is a pile of dry wood under a hide on every mound between Bant and the Lauwers, and for once the people who built it are the people who will be burned if it fails.
Each after his own custom

A day's ride south of Sliesthorp, twelve Franks and twelve Danes are meeting on the bank of the Eider to swear peace, each side after its own custom. Neither side has ever watched the other swear. Both would like one man there who is believed on the other bank.

Twelve of ours. The king's brothers Hankwin and Angandeo. Osfrid from Skane, and two more Osfrids, so that they can be told apart only by their fathers. They swear as we swear. Yours swear on bones in a box. Somebody must tell each side that the other has truly sworn.
Count Wala leads ours. He is the emperor's own cousin, and he has asked me twice whether the Danes will laugh at the relics. I told him no. I have not asked the Danes.

It has been sworn. Nobody laughed. Now two of ours ride south to the emperor's hall with gifts, and what was said on the river bank has to be said again there in the same words. That is harder than it sounds.
Hemming is dead, and his kin are killing one another for the high seat. What the twelve swore still stands at the gate, for as long as there is anyone alive who remembers swearing it.
I was on your coast last summer, on the king's errand. The king is dead. I have a ship and forty men and no errand. I find I would sooner sell a thing than weigh it.
I still have your bronze pound. I use it. It has cost me a good deal of silver, and men trust me, which is new.
Stand witness for both sides, and ask the freedom of the king's gate for your boat
Ask that the oath name merchants: traders of both peoples to cross with their goods in peace
Let the lords swear, and join hands with the Dane who has a ship and no errand

You stand between the two rows and say to each, in its own tongue, that the others have sworn and meant it. It takes a morning. The Franks give you silver and the Danes give you silver, eight hundred pennies' weight between them, and the spokesman has it said at the gate in the wall that your boat passes without the king's toll. The oath itself speaks of kings and borders. It does not mention merchants. Nobody thought of them.

You ask it of the spokesman first and the count second, so that each believes the other thought of it. That the traders of both peoples may cross the border with their goods, and buy and sell in peace. The Danes add it because their king wants his market full. The Franks add it because it costs nothing. It is sworn with the rest. You have four hundred pennies, six timbers of marten from the king's own store, the freedom of the gate, and a guest's right in any Danish harbour: the first merchant the peace was written for.

While the lords swear, you and Ketil sit on an upturned boat and settle it in fewer words. His ship, your markets. He lays down ten sacks of amber and four timbers of marten as his part, and you lay down what a Frisian knows about Dorestat. You join hands on it before his crew. They cheer, mostly because it means they will be paid.

By the emperor's word the Frisian keels of the Rhine mouths are sworn to the coast watch, forty days a summer each, by turns. A boat that serves pays no toll at Dorestat. The counts are not pleased, and the shipmen are counting days.
The mounds from Bant to the Lauwers have sworn a watch among themselves: a fire ready on each, a man awake beside it, and a keel to carry the word. No count was asked.
It was sworn on the Eider, with the rest of the peace, that traders of the Danes and of the Franks may cross the border with their goods and buy and sell unharmed. Twelve men of each people swore it.

The dam at Dorestat on a grey spring morning: a young clerk standing on a cask reading from a strip of parchment, shipmen half listening; in front, a thick-set Frankish count in a red cloak looking down into a small open boat.

A bare dune at the mouth of the Scheldt under a wide pale sky: a pile of driftwood covered with a cowhide; below it four boats drawn up on the sand, two of them flat river barges; a tired Frankish soldier and a farmer with a spear looking out to an empty sea.

A Danish landing crowded with long ships, bows to the shingle, men carrying sacks and coils of rope aboard and stepping masts; in front, a Dane with a gilded cloak pin talking down to a small Frisian boat; a still, bright evening.

A Frisian dwelling mound in spring sun, seen from the creek: turf houses on a green hump, washed wool over the fences, ewes and lambs on the salt grass; an old man with a staff and a woman with a distaff looking at the merchant; nothing on the northern horizon.

Seen from a small boat lying low among sandbanks: a horizon crowded from edge to edge with square sails and oars, a fleet passing along low islands in hard midday light; in the bow a boy shading his eyes, beside him an old Dane who is not surprised.

On top of the mound at Emuthon under a low sky: a cloak spread on the grass with brooches, arm rings, a cup and a few pennies on it; an old law-speaker with a notched tally stick; women taking the pins from their shoulders; long ships on the strand below.

A grey strand at low water: a Dane of about forty seated on a sea chest holding up a small folding balance, silver in one pan and lead weights in the other; an old Frisian facing him; behind, twelve men sitting roped together beside beached long ships.

A river bank in high summer, dust in the air: soldiers and carts crowding to the water, sacks of bread passed down into boats, a dead ox lying in its yoke by the road with the carter standing over it; tents and spears along the far bank.

Inside the count's timber hall at Dorestat on an autumn afternoon, light from the door: an older Frankish lord in a travelling cloak seated in the high chair, a clerk writing at his side, the count standing with folded arms; a shipman in front of them, cap in hand.

A winter night at Dorestat: boats frozen in at the dam under snow, a fire in a storehouse doorway; round it a Frankish clerk, a young Frisian in sheepskin and a Saxon in a hooded cloak, each leaning toward the merchant from a different side.

The cliffs at Bononia at dusk from the sea: a tall old Roman tower in bands of red and pale stone, a fire just lit on its top throwing a path of light over dark water; new long ships at anchor below it; a small boat in front, her crew looking up.

The bank of the Scheldt at Ganda on a cold bright November morning: thirty new tarred ships in a row on the grass, an abbey behind; a very tall old man in a blue cloak, leaning on a stick, with his hand on a ship's stem; lords and monks at a distance; at the end of the row one shorter, deeper hull.

The green by the creek at Emuthon in early summer: the households of the mound standing in a ring with one gap in it, new-shorn sheep beyond, the old law-speaker in the middle with his staff, a widow with a boy of twelve; on the mound behind, a pile of wood under a hide.

A flat river bank in a cold spring wind: twelve Frankish lords on one side with a priest holding a small reliquary, twelve Danes on the other with weapons laid on the ground before them; between the two rows a merchant with a Saxon interpreter at his shoulder; horses and a wagon behind.
